name: Executive order of January 26, 1877 restoring part of the White Mountain reservation to the public domain
nations: Western Apache (the groups named in Docket 22-D)
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It restored to the public domain a rectangle of the White Mountain reservation, 360 by 240 chains, surveyed by Lieutenant E. D. Thomas northeast of the flagstaff of Camp Apache (Royce p. 888, area 601).

Royce cross-refers it to the orders of November 9, 1871, December 14, 1872, August 5, 1873, April 27, 1876 and March 31, 1877, which made and then cut down the White Mountain reservation (Royce p. 889).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission concluded that by six executive orders, naming this order of January 26, 1877, the United States took without compensation Western Apache aboriginal title land inside the enlarged White Mountain reservation, each as of its date, and ordered the acreage and value of each excluded tract determined.

breaches.what: In its opinion the Commission concluded that by successively diminishing the enlarged White Mountain reservation, including by the order of January 26, 1877, the United States wrongfully took additional Western Apache aboriginal title lands as of the dates of the orders.

landTaken: The tract described by the order (360 by 240 chains). No acreage figure was found in a source opened.
compensation: None at the time. The Docket 22-D claim was compromised; the final award of September 12, 1972 (28 Ind. Cl. Comm. 399) awarded $4,900,000 for the Western Apache land claim as a whole, not per tract.
today: The Fort Apache (White Mountain) and San Carlos reservations remain. Whether and how the 1972 award was distributed was not traced.

nationVoice.summary: In 2009 House testimony, Tribal Chairman Ronnie Lupe said the Fort Apache Reservation was established on November 9, 1871 on 1.66 million acres of aboriginal lands the Tribe has occupied since time immemorial, and that the Tribe has kept exclusive use of its aboriginal lands within the boundaries set by the Executive Orders of November 9, 1871 and December 14, 1872.

openQuestions: treaties.json error: presentDayTribes is empty for this record; the White Mountain Apache Tribe should be listed. Not edited.
Whether the whole of area 601 lay inside the Western Apache title area of Finding 11 was not plotted; the Commission names this order expressly, so the finding is treated as about this land.
The White Mountain Apache Tribe's own account of this order was not located.

Audit 2026-11-08: reopened Docket 22-D interlocutory order (OSU 932, conclusion 5 names January 26, 1877; quote exact apart from the scan's line-break hyphen in com-pensation), opinion (OSU 1611) and final award (OSU 1055: $4,900,000, 28 Ind. Cl. Comm. 399); award amount added to compensation. Royce p. 888 text (360 by 240 chains, Lieutenant E. D. Thomas, Camp Apache flagstaff) matches. Double-count check: area 601 is mapped only here (cession-1871-11-09-apache maps 541, 573, 582, 603; cession-1877-03-31-apache maps 602, 603; cession-1886-10-01-apache-western-bands maps 689, the land outside the reservation taken May 1, 1873 under conclusion 4). Conclusion 5 orders a separate acreage and value for each excluded tract as of each order's date, so this is a distinct taking; no sameEventAs.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. A presidential order in 1877 took a surveyed tract near Camp Apache out of the White Mountain reservation and returned it to the public domain.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found this order was one of six by which the United States took Western Apache land inside the reservation without paying for it.
plain.today: The Western Apache claim was settled by a compromise award in 1972. Whether it was distributed was not traced.
